title: The space between who you were and who you're becoming
excerpt: There's a particular kind of grief nobody talks about — the grief of outgrowing a version of yourself you built carefully, for good reasons, over many years.
body:
There's a particular kind of grief nobody talks about — the grief of outgrowing a version of yourself you built carefully, for good reasons, over many years.

We talk about loss in terms of relationships ending, people leaving, things being taken. But there's another kind. The quiet, disorienting loss of a self you no longer recognise as yours.

She was useful, that version of you. She kept things together. She knew how to manage, how to stay small enough to avoid conflict, how to make herself acceptable. She worked hard at it. And she kept you safe.

The trouble is, she's still running the show. Long after the danger has passed.

I see it in every woman I work with. The moment something opens up — a new possibility, a conversation that asks something real of her — and instead of stepping forward, she steps back. Not because she doesn't want it. Because some part of her still believes that wanting things is dangerous.

That's not weakness. That's just habit. Habits built with good reason, at a time when they made sense.

The work isn't about dismantling her, that careful, capable, surviving version of you. It's about letting her rest. About building something alongside her, something that knows it's finally safe to want more.

That transition — from surviving to choosing — is not a moment. It's a practice. And it begins with noticing.
